name: Zucchini / Courgette

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plant zucchini in rich, well-drained soil. Mix a few inches of compost into the bed before you plant, and use raised beds or low mounds if your soil is heavy or stays wet. Good drainage plus plenty of compost gives you healthy, productive plants.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Zucchini grows best in deep, fertile loam that holds steady moisture yet drains freely. Work several inches of compost or well-rotted manure into the bed before planting, since these are organic-matter-hungry plants. Raised beds or mounded hills improve drainage and warm the soil faster in spring. Sandy loams warm early and suit the earliest sowings, while heavy clay holds water and invites root and crown rot, so amend it generously or grow in raised beds.

ph.note_beginner: Zucchini likes soil close to neutral, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and most garden soil is already in range. If you have never tested your soil, an inexpensive test kit tells you whether you need to adjust it.
ph.note_seasoned: Zucchini does best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5. It tolerates a wider band, roughly 5.8 to 7.5, and still produces in mildly alkaline soil, though uptake of iron and manganese tightens as pH climbs. A soil test is the only reliable guide before adding lime or sulfur.

companions.note_beginner: Good companions for squash do one of three things: draw pests away, bring in bees, or feed the soil. Plant a few nasturtiums or marigolds nearby to lure squash bugs off your plants, add flowers like borage to attract the bees that pollinate your squash, and let beans share the bed to enrich the soil. Just give your squash plenty of room, since the plants get big.
companions.note_seasoned: Squash benefits most from companions that pull pests away, feed beneficial insects, or fix nitrogen, rather than from plants packed in tight. Give sprawling vines their room and use companions as a border or light interplanting. The strongest evidence is for nasturtium, with marigold close behind, reducing squash bug and cucumber beetle pressure, while the Three Sisters trio (corn, beans, squash) earns its place through nitrogen, support, and pest confusion. Pollinator flowers like borage and sweet alyssum matter because squash is insect-pollinated, so anything that keeps bees working improves fruit set. Several herb and flower pairings here are traditional rather than trial-proven, and are labeled accordingly.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Part of the classic Three Sisters planting. The tall stalks support climbing beans, and growing corn, beans, and squash together can confuse squash pests.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Pole beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans pull nitrogen from the air and feed the soil, which hungry squash appreciate. Let them climb the corn in a Three Sisters bed.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: These easy flowers lure squash bugs and beetles away from your squash, and research backs it up. Bonus: the flowers are edible.

good_seasoned.name: Corn
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The structural backbone of the Three Sisters. Tall corn gives pole beans a living trellis, and interplanting corn, beans, and squash makes it harder for squash pests to zero in on the planting.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Three Sisters polyculture; corn-as-support and squash-as-groundcover are well established in extension guidance.

good_seasoned.name: Pole beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beans fix atmospheric nitrogen and ease the fertilizer demand of hungry squash, and in a Three Sisters bed they climb the corn while squash shades the soil below.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation and Three Sisters companion structure are extension-supported.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The strongest flower pairing for squash: research shows nasturtium can pull squash bugs off the crop, and an Iowa study found it reduced squash bug and cucumber beetle damage. The flowers are also edible.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: UMN states the practice is supported by research; cites an Iowa study on squash bug and cucumber beetle damage.

good_seasoned.name: Marigold
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted with squash to deter pests. The evidence is mixed overall, but the same Iowa study that backs nasturtium also found marigolds reduced squash bug and cucumber beetle damage, so it earns a likely rating here.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: UMN reports an Iowa study showing marigolds reduced squash bug and cucumber beetle damage, while noting marigold results are inconsistent generally.

good_seasoned.name: Sweet alyssum
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low carpet of sweet alyssum draws hoverflies and other beneficial insects. A Florida study found alyssum increased natural enemies of aphids on squash, and the blooms also feed pollinators.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: UMN cites a Florida study in which sweet alyssum increased natural enemies of aphids on squash.

good_seasoned.name: Borage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A classic pollinator magnet. Its bee-friendly blue flowers help keep pollinators working the squash blooms, which matters because zucchini is insect-pollinated. The pairing is traditional rather than trial-proven.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Well-documented traditional pollinator companion; squash-specific benefit not from a controlled trial.

good_seasoned.name: Sage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: An aromatic herb long planted near squash to discourage squash bugs. Treat this as traditional garden lore rather than a tested effect for squash.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic-herb pest-deterrence is widely repeated folk practice; no squash-specific trial support.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep potatoes in a separate bed. Both plants are big and hungry and will compete for food and space.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Plant fennel on its own, away from squash. It grows large and may crowd or stunt nearby vegetables.

bad_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both potatoes and squash are vigorous, hungry plants that compete hard for the same water, nutrients, and ground space, so most growers keep them in separate beds. The caution is traditional rather than trial-proven.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Widely repeated competition-based caution; not from a controlled companion trial.

bad_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is the classic give-it-its-own-bed plant. It is reputed to release compounds that can suppress nearby vegetables, and it grows large enough to crowd sprawling squash. The allelopathy evidence is mostly observational, so treat this as traditional caution.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel allelopathy toward garden vegetables is largely observational; squash-specific effect uncertain.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Harden off indoor-started squash over 7 to 10 days, easing them into direct sun and wind before transplanting. Handle the rootball gently at planting, because squash resents root disturbance and a checked seedling can sulk for weeks.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started seedlings indoors, set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they adjust to sun and wind. Be gentle with the roots when you plant, since squash does not like having its roots disturbed.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Because squash resents root disturbance, direct sowing once the soil warms past 60°F, ideally 70°F, is the simplest and most reliable method, and direct-sown plants quickly catch up to transplants. Start seeds indoors only to gain two to three weeks in a short season, using larger cells (3 inch or bigger) and setting plants out before the roots circle the pot.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way to grow zucchini is to sow seeds right where they will grow, once the soil is warm (about 70°F). Squash grows fast and does not transplant happily, so direct sowing usually works best. Start seeds indoors only if your season is short, and move them outside while they are still small.

recommended.name: Black Beauty
recommended.recommended_note: Classic dark-green heirloom; compact, open-pollinated, and dependably productive.

recommended.name: Costata Romanesco
recommended.recommended_note: Ribbed Italian heirloom prized for nutty flavor; large, sprawling plants that reward room.

recommended.name: Raven
recommended.recommended_note: Compact dark-green hybrid that suits containers and small beds.

recommended.name: Goldrush
recommended.recommended_note: Bright golden-yellow hybrid with uniform, easy-to-spot fruit.

recommended.name: Cocozelle
recommended.recommended_note: Striped Italian heirloom with firm, flavorful fruit.

recommended.name: Dunja
recommended.recommended_note: Vigorous organic hybrid with an open, easy-to-pick habit.

varieties.note_seasoned: For a first garden almost any zucchini succeeds, so choose by space and color. Compact bush habits like Raven or Dunja fit small beds and containers and keep airflow open to slow powdery mildew, while sprawling heirlooms like Costata Romanesco and Cocozelle reward more room with exceptional flavor. Mixing a green type with a yellow one such as Goldrush makes fruit easier to spot before it oversizes. Black Beauty remains the reliable green standard.
varieties.note_beginner: Zucchini is forgiving, so pick a variety by the space you have. Bush types like Raven stay compact and do well in pots, while classics like Black Beauty are reliable in a garden bed. A yellow type such as Goldrush is easy to spot at picking size.

UF/IFAS Northwest District Horticulture Vegetable Garden Planting Dates (Florida Panhandle)
UF/IFAS SP 103/VH021 Florida Vegetable Gardening Guide
UGA Extension Bulletin 577 (Vegetable Garden Planting Chart)

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Zucchini is famous for overwhelming a garden, so resist sowing the whole crop at once. A first sowing after your last frost, then a second about three weeks later, spreads the harvest and keeps vigorous plants coming as the originals tire. The real payoff is late season: squash vine borer and powdery mildew often take down the first planting by midsummer, so a replacement sown in early to midsummer, counting back from your first fall frost so it has time to mature, frequently outproduces the spring crop on cleaner, less stressed plants.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You rarely need more than one or two zucchini plants at a time, and a single planting can feed you for weeks. For a steadier supply, sow a few seeds now and a few more about three weeks later. A second planting in summer is a smart backup, since pests and disease often wear out the first plants by late summer.

northern_tier.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh from T1 (no legacy zones{} to de-multiplex). Direct-sow-dominant cucurbit: plant_out is the after-frost direct-sow window once soil >=70F at 2 in (UMN); start_indoors is the 3-week transplant-early lead used at the short-season cold end (z3-z5) to gain time. Single continuous summer window capped by the fall-frost runway; succession is the 3-week cadence (UMD/UMN), not a spring/fall split. Fall replacement (squash vine borer / powdery mildew) sits inside the same continuous window, counted back from first frost. Region-specific window per A5; not analogized from another region.

se_gulf.plantings_provenance: UGA Extension Bulletin 577 home-garden planting chart (Squash, bush, 50-55 days: spring Apr 1-May 15, fall Aug 1-20, middle Georgia) plus Circular 943 (make a second planting 2-3 weeks after the first in spring; plant cucumbers and squash for fall no later than Aug 31). The Southeast/Gulf is a true SPRING + FALL split: virus pressure, squash vine borer, and mid-summer heat curtail production in late summer, leaving a no-plant gap between the spring crop's heat-driven end and the fall sowing. The chart's own zone notes shift the dates (south Georgia ~ z9 earlier in spring/later in fall; north-Georgia edge ~ z8 later in spring/earlier in fall). succession_spring + succession_fall per second_planting spec v1.1; the mid-summer no-plant month renders heat_pause. Region-specific per A5; the fall window is a SE finding and is NOT carried to ca_interior or warm_arid.

9.succession_continuous: Mar 15, Apr 5, Apr 26, May 17, Jun 7, Jun 28

ca_interior.plantings_provenance: UC ANR Pub 7245 (Summer Squash Production in California) plus Sacramento and Santa Clara/Marin County Master Gardener charts: Central Valley squash is direct-sown once soil reaches ~70 degrees F (Mar 15 safe without protection; soil-warm late Mar through July set-out), producing through summer and tapering in fall on aphid-transmitted virus and whitefly pressure. This is one continuous warm-season window, not a spring/fall split: no mid-summer no-plant gap is documented, and zucchini is heat-loving, so peak heat is a window edge, not a heat_pause. succession_continuous per second_planting spec v1.1 (window_type continuous). Region-specific per A5.

ca_north_coast.plantings_provenance: UC Marin Master Gardener squash guide plus UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (North/North Coast column): on the cool maritime coast squash is seeded indoors in March and set out from mid-April through June (some to July), once nights are above 55 degrees F, and bears until weather cools in fall. The marine layer makes this region heat-LIMITED (a later start, a slower bloom), not heat-stalled, so there is no heat_pause and the window is one continuous run. succession_continuous. Region-specific per A5; the coastal behavior is the inverse of ca_interior at the same hardiness band.

ca_south_coast.plantings_provenance: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (South Coast column) plus Los Angeles County Master Gardener guidance (wait until warm soil, roughly end of April, to set out squash): the mild South Coast supports one long continuous warm-season window from spring set-out into late fall, heat-limited by the marine layer rather than stalled. No heat_pause; not year_round (a frost-tender annual with a cool-season slowdown). succession_continuous. Region-specific per A5.

ca_desert.plantings_provenance: UC ANR Pub 7245 (early-spring desert squash is sown in the cool early months -- the publication notes December and January sowings for the southern desert valleys -- with main production in spring and acreage falling off sharply in fall under aphid-transmitted virus and silverleaf whitefly) plus UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Desert Valleys column, Imperial/Coachella). The low desert is a SPRING + FALL split: an early-spring crop set before the heat, a summer too hot for reliable fruit set and heavy with whitefly/virus, then a fall crop. succession_spring + succession_fall; the mid-summer no-plant months render heat_pause. Region-specific per A5; distinct from low_desert_az (AZ) by institution and by slightly milder z10 timing.

warm_arid.region_label: Warm Arid: Southern New Mexico & West Texas
warm_arid.plantings_provenance: NMSU Circular 457 statewide planting-date table (southern band, Las Cruces/Dona Ana ~ zone 8) plus Texas A&M AgriLife far-west Texas guidance: the southern New Mexico / west Texas warm-arid band at zone 8 (higher elevation than the Sonoran low desert) runs one long warm-season window after the spring frost through to the fall frost. Unlike the low desert (AZ1005, two short seasons around a brutal summer gap), no T1 documents a mid-summer no-plant break for this higher-elevation z8 band, so it is authored continuous, mirroring the green-beans warm_arid z8 finding. succession_continuous. Region-specific per A5. FLAG: if the release-lane NMSU read shows a desert-style summer no-plant gap at z8, this would split; authored continuous on the evidence in hand.

low_desert_az.plantings_provenance: U of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005 (Vegetable Planting Calendar for Maricopa County, peer-reviewed): Summer Squash (60-90 days) is seeded in two distinct seasons -- spring (~Feb 15-Mar 15, extendable to mid-April per the UA low-desert summer-survival guidance if established before the heat) and fall (~Aug 15-Sep 15) -- around a summer too hot for fruit set and heavy with whitefly. AZ1005 states the low desert has two optimal planting seasons (spring and fall) because few annuals thrive through the summer extreme; the cucurbit rows (cucumber, summer squash) show exactly this split. AZ1615 (Yuma) corroborates the two short production windows. succession_spring + succession_fall; the May-Aug no-plant stretch renders heat_pause. Region-specific per A5; zone 9 only (the desert fold at z10 is served by ca_desert).

fl_peninsula.plantings_provenance: UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions Summer Squash page (summer squash does not grow in Florida during the heat of summer; in North Florida it is grown Feb-Apr and Aug-Sep; in central/south Florida the windows shift earlier into fall and through the mild winter) plus the Florida Vegetable Gardening Guide (VH021) inverted-calendar framing. On the peninsula (z10-11) the growing season is inverted: the cool half (roughly late summer through spring) is continuous for squash, and the Jun-Aug heat is the off-season. This is one continuous inverted window rather than a frost-bracketed spring/fall split, so succession_continuous applies and the summer off-season renders season_over (a frost-free region's bounded off-season token, not heat_pause, per the locked rule). Region-specific per A5. z11 is frost-free, so resolved_from is null.

11.succession_continuous: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct

hawaii_tropical.plantings_provenance: U of Hawaii CTAHR home-garden planting guidance (Bulletin B-91 and CTAHR crop guidelines): zucchini can be grown through much of the year in Hawaii, favored at cooler elevations and on drier leeward sites, with wet-season disease and insect pressure the practical limiter. Authored as BOUNDED-CONTINUOUS, NOT year_round: no CTAHR source located that explicitly states continuous year-round zucchini cultivation, and per the locked rule a frost-free zone 11 alone is not sufficient to declare year_round (onion and zinnia precedents). succession_continuous. resolved_from is null (frost-free). *** STRUCTURAL FLAG FOR CLAUDE CODE: if the release-lane CTAHR fetch finds an explicit continuous / year-round zucchini statement, upgrade this cell to year_round (the basil/zinnia Hawaii pattern) and log a blocks_launch:false open finding; default authored here is bounded-continuous, climate-and-source honest, with no fabricated source_quote. ***

pollinator_notes_seasoned: Zucchini is monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a single plant sets fruit with no second variety needed. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and pollen must move from the male to the female blooms. Poor pollination, common in cool, wet, or pollinator-scarce conditions, shows up as small fruit that yellow and rot at the blossom end, or as misshapen, pinched squash. Early-season male flowers often open and drop before the first females appear, which is normal. Plant flowers nearby and avoid spraying open blooms to keep pollinators working, and hand-pollinate with a small brush if fruit set stalls.
pollinator_notes_beginner: Each zucchini plant has both male and female flowers, so you only need one plant to get fruit. Bees move the pollen between flowers, so anything that brings bees to your garden helps. If your early squash stay small and rot at the tip, the flowers usually were not pollinated well, often in cool or rainy weather. It tends to sort itself out as more flowers open and bees get busy.
